Anna Pávlovna’s exclamation was intended to set Prince Vasíli at
ease. He, however, feeling that the conversation with her was becoming
too personal, and that he could not fathom her intimate feelings, and
perhaps, too, a bit ashamed of his own, but conscious that he was not
the only one, looked at his watch and withdrew his hand from the
chair-arm, saying he had to go. Anna Pávlovna Schérer standing on the
threshold, continued to smile, as if she were still speaking to
herself. She said, in the same dry tone as she had spoken about the
Empress:

“I am going to take a walk…. I have scarcely been out of doors
for a week.”

She turned to go, but suddenly, as if she were remembering something,
she paused and looked at the prince with some embarrassment, as if
wishing to say something, but not knowing how to begin, and he, not
knowing how to end, said, with a sigh:

“Ah, but I’m so sorry to be so long, but it’s so hot.”

Anna Pávlovna Schérer, after a moment’s hesitation, said:

“Very well, then, and good-bye, dear friend. If you require advice,
you know where I am.”

And she went out, closing the door behind her. The prince, turning
to the princess, said:

“I have something to tell you. Your mother, I learned only this
morning, has come back to St. Petersburg, and she, like all the other
ladies, expects you.”

Anna Pávlovna Schérer was the first to arrive at the reception, and
so, by her punctuality, was the first to be greeted. She had not
arrived before the Empress Márya Fëdorovna; the Empress, however, was
sorry to see her and, in a voice that sounded strange and somewhat
strangely, said, in Russian, good-bye to her, and invited her to
dinner. Anna Pávlovna Schérer, with a very unconvincing smile, and as if
she had no need to be served, and as if the Empress had not even asked
her to dinner, sat down on the sofa with two ladies who had also
arrived a few minutes before her. As she was about to take a seat, a
footman was sent to her to notify her that Her Majesty was waiting
for her. Anna Pávlovna rose and said she would follow the Empress,
taking the hand of the footman, dressed in a white dress, which in that
year was very elegant, and which, as it was at that time not a custom
to wear a fur cloak, she put on on her way.

She was met by the Empress, who was sitting in the garden, where
the Empress Márya Fëdorovna had gone after the reception, in order to
write a letter. A few minutes after Anna Pávlovna sat down, the Empress
said to her, in a mild and kindly voice, and with a smile on her face:

“Tell me, Anna Pávlovna, did you not come to receive me?”

Anna Pávlovna Schérer, very politely, with a smile, but without the
least consciousness of her own, said:

“No, I did not, because I had not come here at all. I went to the
Empress Márya Fëdorovna.”

The Empress Márya Fëdorovna, who was sitting on a solid garden chair,
with its arms spread out, and which she had given to the Empress, and
which she always used, said to the Empress with a smile so different
from that with which she had smiled to Anna Pávlovna Schérer:

“Anna Pávlovna is always so kind and obliging. You know, my dear
friend, I am constantly in a hurry. I have so many things to do, and I
am always in a hurry. I am always in a hurry, and I am sorry to be in a
hurry.”

She suddenly remembered that she had not yet said a word about
herself and the Empress, and then, with a smile as if to say, “You
see, I am in a hurry,” she said to the Empress, “I have come
to ask you to notify me of the hour of the supper and the name of the
guests. I am always in a hurry.”

The Empress, with a smile, and with an air of being in a hurry, said,
in a voice that sounded strange, as if she were not sure whether she
had spoken correctly, and as if it were impossible to be in a hurry, she
said:

“I have already sent the announcement, and I have already sent
the invitations.”

Anna Pávlovna, with a smile, and with a voice that sounded strange,
as if she did not know why she was in a hurry, said:

“Very well, I am already informed. I was informed of the hour
of the supper and the names of the guests, but I don’t wish to be in a
hurry.”

The Empress, with a smile, said:

“As you please, Anna Pávlovna—when and where will you be
in a hurry?—as you please, Anna Pávlovna.”

Anna Pávlovna, with a smile, and with an air of being in a hurry, said:

“I am sorry, but I have to be in a hurry. I must go.”

And with a smile and with an air of being in a hurry, she went away.

Pávlovna’s remarks, because he was not the least interested in them
and had already made up his mind not to acknowledge them or to give in
to her pathetic influence. He answered in an indifferent voice that he
did not like Anatole, for he was not quite sure that he liked anybody!

In the middle of the conversation a footman presented a card to the
prince, and he went away. He was followed by Anna Pávlovna, who at
first went up to the prince, made a few more polite remarks, and then
added:

“The general will be pleased to receive you at his house this
evening. He is full of the greatest love and gratitude toward the
Empress. He would be pleased to hear your ideas.”

reset on the sofa. There was a moment of silence, in which one could
hear the soft beating of the music, which was played by a small orchestra
in the top story of the palace, and then the prince exclaimed:

“I think we must be going, do you not? I am losing time. I must send
you a message, dear Anna Pávlovna, that I wish you joy of your health.
Come in one day when you feel better and let me know how you feel. My
family are well. Good-bye.”

Anna Pávlovna rose. But Prince Vasíli Kurágin, before she could
reach the door, seized her by the hand.

“Not you, and not them. I shall not send it,” he said, turning to her.
“I fear you do not know so well how to receive the ‘faithful servants’
of the Empress and high officials as I do. If you do not wish to send
the message, I will send it. But you must promise not to send it
now. You are not so good as to send it till the next day. I shall not
be so ill as to send you a message. Good-bye.”

Anna Pávlovna drew back her hand, and, before she had reached the steps,
he repeated:

“Good-bye. Please do not send it.”

She turned her face towards the prince, and he could see that in her
eyes was the same solemn and, at the same time, tender look which
he had met there sometimes before.

She bowed to him, but the prince added, and without a word:

“Good-bye.”

determined, in spite of her habit, to conceal from anyone the importance
of this meeting.

Significantly and frequently her eyes glanced along the walls at
gilt frames of paintings by Nicolai and Rembrandt. The Prince Vasíli
Kurágin who was present at the reception, in spite of being a regular
at the highest level of Petersburg, had never seen anything like
these pictures. They were in the private collection of the Count
Schérer, Anna Pávlovna’s husband. And Anna Pávlovna, to show the
impression made by these works on those present, continued to speak
of them as she would have spoken of the court or the wars, without
reference to the person addressed.

The prince, as she had expected, listened with quiet interest and
simulated indifference, answered her with a few words expressive of
his agreement or displeasure, and then, when she had said all she
wanted to say, and as if he were tired, he rose from his seat and said
good-bye, saying, as he went out:

“I shall certainly be delighted to see you at the fete.”

Anna Pávlovna Schérer, in her great room, with its skin-coloured trimmings,
and the frescoes of the great masters, had also received the Count
Constantin Schérer, her husband, and had her servant, the Countess
Baroness, deliver to him the invitation to the fete. Though she had
made this acquaintance some time ago, the Count Schérer, for whom she
was a favorite, always at the right moment, was not ashamed to show
himself. He was an excellent conversationalist and was with a
courtierlike solemnity, which he did not lose sight of, turning to
Anna Pávlovna with the question, “What are you going to do next?
You are still unwell, and all that I have heard from Wintzingerode
concerning you is that you have pricked your finger on a splinter of a
candlestick. You know I am never at a loss for something to do.”

“I do indeed have a headache,” said Anna Pávlovna, “but I will go
over and talk with my dear Wintzingerode, and I want to see the baron
before I leave. And above all I have to go to see my young friend
the Countess Baroness. I will be with you in a moment.”

So she left the room and passed down a corridor (the Count Schérer
was lying on his sofa) to the door, opened it, bowed, and said to the
Countess Baroness:

“Good evening, my dear.”

The Countess Baroness, who was standing at the window, turned and
looked at Anna Pávlovna Schérer smilingly, with that smile which, when
one thinks of her, is always associated with her name, and she answered:

“Good evening, Anna Pávlovna, I have not seen you for some time.
How are you, I am so glad to see you?”

“Oh, we are just recovering from la grippe,” answered Anna Pávlovna
Schérer, “but I shall be with you and Wintzingerode very soon.”

“Oh, that is just right, the Count Schérer is not at home, you wished
to go to him, I wish to go to Wintzingerode, we are good friends, Wintzingerode
and I, I have a headache, and I am afraid I will not be able to attend
the fete. I have not yet seen Juvenal, Wintzingerode, Pissaré, you and
the bonnet Madame de Montmorency gave me, and I am waiting for the
Countess Sophia to talk to us all. I wish you a good evening.”

left the room, went on to the other room where she was sure to find
Wintzingerode. She was, as it were, a little musical instrument,
beautifully tuned, and, as in the case of musical instruments, the
tuning would not last long, and if one stopped playing, it would
bitterly complain: “You have not played for some time.”

Wintzingerode and the Count Schérer had been good friends for a long
time. Their friendship had begun with a baron’s commission, and there
had always been between them an equal respect and trust. They all
knew each other and were well acquainted with the most secret, the
wildest and, as it were, the unconscious secrets of the best society,
which, as a rule, was not capable of maintaining friendship. It was
difficult to describe to Anna Pávlovna Schérer what the Count Schérer
and she had seen, heard, or done, and even the Count Schérer did not
know much about the grand old life at Madame de Montmorency’s, which
was so full of theatrical, social, and political intrigues.

Wintzingerode, in a well-known suit of gray, and with his bandaged
fingers and with the ribbon of the Order of St. George round his neck,
was sitting in the same chair in which he had sat on that first day
at the Countess Baroness’s when he had feared that there would be no
service. He sang a song from the “Forty Years,” then, in an
expression of profound irony, he spoke to Anna Pávlovna Schérer
of the Empress Márya Fëdorovna, his old friend, with whom he was
always in touch.

She was a monarch, Anna Pávlovna Schérer, not only a princess and
lady, but also an equal of the empress, wearied neither by the serfs or
the mob, nor by her own people, or the people of the Holy Roman Empire,
but by the combative, energetic, and valiant spirit of the first Russian
emperor. She was a true, real, and worthy woman, a man, a Russian, and
only an emperor.

Anna Pávlovna Schérer, after a moment of silence, did not, as usual,
make any response, but, without taking her eyes off Wintzingerode, she
added:

“The Empress was all that was good and right, a good and noble Russian.
Our Emperor is virtuous, adoring and noble. I have faith in him and in
the future of Russia, just as I have faith in the fate of the world and
in God, who has given us a great task, and we shall carry it out bravely.
I know that the world is kind, and will always be, because it is the
fate of Russia to be the world’s protector. Our Emperor will be the
greatest and most powerful, the most glorious and beneficent emperor
on earth. Because he will be great he will always be in the world,
and he will always be the Russian protector. The Emperor will one day
be as great as Alexander the Great, and do me a favor and be as great
as Alexander himself, who nursed the world’s hope through many dark
days and when all was lost. If you do not say nor think that the world
is good and kind, you will not see the future as I see it, and I will
show you how the future must be. You know what I do. I am a poor
invalid, and I receive the Empress’s kind help, the help of the
Dowager Empress, and that is enough: I do not wish more. I do not wish
to be a princess and a lady, I wish only to be admiral and a sovereign,
the most powerful and the most great sovereign. I wish to be the
sovereign, the wife, and the mother of a great lord. I wish to be the
wise and virtuous Empress of Russia. I believe that I am right and in
the right, and that at the same time I shall be happy. In the future
Russia, as always, will be a great and powerful country, and our Emperor,
our sovereign, will be the greatest and most powerful, and the most
glorious and the most kind of emperor on earth.... I am a great Russian,
and a grand lady, and I want to be a sovereign or the wife of a sovereign,
and I want to be a Russian, a princess, and a lady, and I shall be,
and I shall be able to do so, and I shall be equal to my Emperor and
his vocation, and our future will be good and kind, and it shall be,
and it will be because I have faith in the future, in Russia, in the
Empress, and in God, who will help, and you will be the first to help
me, and I want—no, I must tell you, and I will, and I will explain
every detail of my life and how I have lived, and how I want to live,
and I will make you understand, and if you do not understand I shall
write to the Empress, and the Lord Empress will want to speak to you,
and I will be able to do so. I will now be very quiet, so that I can
listen to what you have to say. Don’t laugh, I have not been far
from you, and I have heard all that you have said. But you have not said
everything, and I must tell you still more. I know who are those
two men, and I will be able to explain everything to you, and you will
understand, and Wintzingerode knows everything! You will not be able
to help an old invalid and a woman like me to explain myself, but I
shall be able, and I shall be able to explain, and I will explain,
and I will think, and I will make up my mind, and you will be able to
help. I have not time to speak in a long letter, and I have not the

The prince, with the same exulting indifference which admitted of
no rejoinder, returned to the point he had previously raised, and
was addressing, not herself, but the world in general:

“Is not it extraordinary that during the last twenty years the
Empress has always chosen to make her retina shine on the thousands of
young persons on whom Russia has found it necessary to live? Has it not
appeared to you an extraordinary circumstance, since the Empress is so
happy and the children of the worthy Walter, in spite of everything,
remain ever and ever the same, and you as father have lost all your
appetite for life?”

Bending to a sideboard, Anna Pávlovna began hunting for sugar and
butter, which she lay down before the prince. Having touched the
footman at the door, she placed a forbidding letter from the empress
on the table and secretly watched her guest, who had remained seated.

“Here is a letter from the Empress. She praises you. I must write her
the very same things. I promised that I would.”

Prince Vasíli, anxiously looking over the letter, shuddered at
reading the words on the flyleaf.

“Why is my daughter advanced?” said he, whose indifferent and arrogant
smile was replaced by an air of cold, profound, and unalterable
indifference. “She is only born to be a schemer. She brings
happiness to no one, but only distresses and threatens. Look, I have
not been in service with pregnant women, but I know, from the past,
that the Empress’ judgement on the Parisian wombs, is not good.” He
looked in at the footman, who was drawing in a corner the toilet service
and leaving it to be cleared by the footman. “I do not care about words.
I only want to know the truth. How long has the Empress Fëdorovna been
sick? How is her health? If she has not recovered, she will inevitably
die, and if that is so, why has she elevated my daughter who is, as I
said, nothing but a schemer to be at the head of our army? Why has she
made her my daughter if she does not wish to surrender to her? I
detest deceits. I could not be consoled in the matter and would not be
consoled for ever. How long has the Empress been sick? She has not
recovered? I have already given her my answer: My only wish has become
her. If my depraved daughter does not listen to me, I shall take one of
her hands as a pledge and bring her before the Archangel Michael and
the Heavenly Father and demand that He give us the conduct and the
might that will avenge us. Thou, God, knoweth the heart.”

At this moment the sale of the tennis and racquet set of the Princess
Sophy ended, the Empress Fëdorovna, accompanied by the Prince Menshikov,
had arrived. In view of this she was engaged in no longer important
conversations, and Anna Pávlovna suddenly left her guests.

We continue our familiar story. The Empress Fëdorovna, with the
beautiful Princess among the peasants, had reached the gates of
Novocherkassk and Florina Kurágin greeted her with a bouquet of flowers.
She did not recognize the Princess and stopped to look at her.

“Well, how do you do, dear Mama? Is it good to get a breath of the
fresh air? We have set off from Maydorf.”

All this was repeated towards the Empress Fëdorovna, but she could not
understand why these peasants, whom she visited once a year, were so
good and full of life. They had so little to give, and for what? One
needs strength, she was the Empress of Russia, and she was the Empress
of Russia! Why, then, are they so good?

The Empress Fëdorovna returned to Petersburg, but not to the Empress
Fëdorovna. Her younger daughter, Sophia, had taken the place of
her mother, and this was the first time that the Empress Fëdorovna had
left Petersburg without her. She had left with the Princess
Sophyfëdorovna. And so, without a personal introduction, the Princess
Sophyfëdorovna, who was the wife of Count Vladimir Kurágin, was the
Empress of Russia.

After the Empress’ quick departure, the Empress’ train forward met the
Princess Sophia with the Princess, and for the next half hour the
empress’ train and the Princess Sophia’s train, which was ten minutes
farther, talked to each other, to be told that the Princess was not
coming, and in a few minutes they separated. The Empress had been
thinking that the Princess had not come because Count Vladimir was
not fit for the journey. Looking at her, the Empress thought: “Why
have Count Vladimir’s eyes become such as they are? He was so fine
and beautiful in their time. And what a capricious little one he is!
When Count Vladimir fancies he is in distress, he is preoccupied with
his troubles and cares by day and night, and day and night he thinks of
nothing else. His thoughts are always the same, and I have lost count
of how many he has in one night, thinking and sleeping at the same time.
But when he wakes up at morning he is well, and he is, as I look at him,
as I have looked at him for so many years, as beautiful and good as he
used to be. His well-being, which has been furthered by my attentions
and the care of his grandmamma, so very able, clever, and good, has
assured that nothing could affect him. But he does not always feel
himself well. His thought is his life, and the instigator of his life
is not he himself but the wife, the Princess Sophia, and the welfare
of the young Princess Sophia is his only thought. In the morning
thought dictates to him what he must do in the evening, and the rules
and decisions of his life follow him in a distance of one thousand
keys. The Princess Sophia, who is so fine and so intelligent, so gentle
and so charming, is talking in her soul, and in answer to her thoughts
and prayers, her son is not fit for the journey. I talk to my poor
father, my dear father, I who will always be his only child, and in
his reply I hear only the sharp sting of the Repka. At the age of
nineteen years he has come to us as if he were not twenty-one, and for
the next three years he will be a poor boy, pale, sickening, and\n miserable. He is only a boy, and a sweet little boy. If he dies now,
how many years of distress will be mine? So that he may live and die,
I must watch over him, and I am sad! My poor Count Vladimir, my
honest, good, kindly, and modest friend, the reproach of truth to my
dear father, my devoted son, my dear father’s favorite and Count
Vladimir, because that lovely and devoted little thing, and the
daughter of Count Vassíly, the younger sister of the Princess
Antónia, Otto, and Shvóshka, is not fit to travel. And Count Vassíly
does not agree.”

The Princess Sophia, standing at the window, thought:

“Irresistibly, very wildly goes that Count Vladimir, another little
cavalcade, and his mother. And I am to give him a good go. And what
has just happened? My husband has made me an offer to take him
home. He will not go. But what has resulted from it? He is able to
fit for service, he will take his place among us in a few days. I am
only distressed that Count Vladimir can never go to see the Empress
Márya Fëdorovna in Russia.”
